title: NCL Mine Surveyor Mock 03
pattern: 100 MCQs, 100 marks, 90 min, NO negative marking

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: Tachometric surveying is preferred over chain surveying when:
options: The ground is flat and open
The ground is rough, undulating, or obstructed
questions.solution: Tachometry is ideal for rough, undulating, or obstructed terrain where direct chaining is difficult or inaccurate.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The accuracy of stadia tachometry is typically:
questions.solution: Stadia tachometry typically achieves accuracy of 1 in 500 to 1 in 1000, suitable for preliminary surveys.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: In tachometry, if the staff is held tilted, the measured distance will be:
questions.solution: A tilted staff gives a larger stadia interval, making the computed distance longer than the true distance.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The 'subtense bar' is typically:
questions.solution: A standard subtense bar is 2 m long, precisely calibrated and mounted horizontally.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: In the subtense bar method, the distance is calculated as:
questions.solution: D = b / (2 tan(θ/2)), where b is the bar length (2 m) and θ is the measured horizontal angle.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: A subtense bar is most useful for:
options: Short to medium accurate distance measurement
questions.solution: Subtense bar is useful for short to medium distances (up to ~200 m) with high accuracy.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: Tachometric methods are extensively used in mine surveying for:
options: Rapid detailing of benches, dump profiles, and stope surveying
questions.solution: Tachometry is widely used in mines for rapid profiling of benches, dumps, high walls, and underground openings.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The 'stadia constant' K is given by:
options: f/i, where f = focal length of objective and i = stadia hair interval
questions.solution: K = f/i, where f is the focal length of the objective and i is the distance between stadia hairs at the focal plane.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: For K to be exactly 100, the ratio f/i must be:
questions.solution: When f/i = 100, the stadia interval factor K equals exactly 100.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: In tachometric surveying, the vertical angle is measured to determine:
options: The height difference and to correct the horizontal distance
questions.solution: The vertical angle is used both to compute the height difference and to reduce the slope distance to horizontal distance.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The advantage of the tangential method over the stadia method is:
options: Higher accuracy, especially at shorter distances
questions.solution: The tangential method offers higher accuracy than stadia at shorter distances because it uses direct angular measurements.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: In stadia tachometry, the staff must be held:
questions.solution: The staff must be held perfectly vertical for accurate stadia readings; otherwise, the distance will be in error.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: Tachometric surveying eliminates the need for:
options: Direct chaining or taping of distances
questions.solution: Tachometry replaces direct distance measurement by chaining/taping with optical distance determination.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: A 'stadia diaphragm' with three horizontal hairs is used to:
options: Read three staff readings (upper, middle, lower) to determine stadia interval
questions.solution: The stadia diaphragm has upper, middle, and lower hairs; the difference between upper and lower readings gives the stadia interval.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The 'tachometric constant' is the product of:
questions.solution: The tachometric constant K = f/i (focal length of objective divided by stadia hair interval).

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: A 'control survey' establishes:
options: A network of precisely located points as a reference framework
questions.solution: Control surveys establish a network of accurately located horizontal and vertical control points.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: Triangulation is a method of horizontal control that uses:
options: Measurement of angles in a network of triangles
questions.solution: Triangulation determines positions by measuring angles in a network of interconnected triangles.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: In a triangulation network, the 'base line' is:
options: The longest side in the network
A precisely measured line from which other distances are computed trigonometrically
questions.solution: The base line is measured with the highest precision and serves as the scale reference for the entire triangulation network.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The 'strength of figure' in triangulation refers to:
options: The physical strength of the survey marker
The geometric quality of the triangle shapes affecting accuracy
questions.solution: Strength of figure describes the geometric quality of triangle shapes; well-conditioned triangles give better accuracy.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: A well-conditioned triangle in triangulation has angles between:
questions.solution: Well-conditioned triangles have all angles between 30° and 120° for optimal geometric strength.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The 'strength of figure' factor R is given by:
options: R = δ₁² + δ₁δ₂ + δ₂² (where δ are the factors from the triangle)
questions.solution: R = D + C where D = δ₁² + δ₁δ₂ + δ₂² and C depends on the number of stations; smaller R means stronger figure.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: In triangulation, 'station adjustment' ensures:
options: The sum of angles around a station equals 360°
questions.solution: Station adjustment distributes angular misclosure so the sum of angles meeting at a station equals exactly 360°.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: A 'geodetic triangle' on the earth's surface has angles that sum to:
questions.solution: On a curved earth, triangle angles sum to 180° + spherical excess; the excess depends on the triangle area.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: Spherical excess is:
options: The amount by which the sum of geodetic triangle angles exceeds 180°
Equal to the base line error
questions.solution: Spherical excess E = (A × 180°) / (R² × sin 1"), where A is the triangle area on the ellipsoid.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: A 'satellite station' in triangulation is a station that:
options: Is not connected to the main triangulation network directly
questions.solution: A satellite station is a supplementary station observed from the main network but not forming part of the primary triangle chain.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The 'subtense' method is used at satellite stations to determine:
options: The coordinates of the satellite station from observed angles to main stations
questions.solution: At satellite stations, angles are observed to surrounding main network points, and the station position is computed by intersection.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: Trilateration is a method of control survey that uses:
questions.solution: Trilateration determines positions by measuring distances (typically with EDM) between control stations.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: An advantage of trilateration over triangulation is:
options: No requirement for inter-visibility between stations (angles not needed)
questions.solution: Trilateration does not require angle measurement, so stations need not be mutually visible (only line of sight for EDM).

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: GPS (Global Positioning System) in mine surveying is used for:
options: Establishing and densifying horizontal control networks
questions.solution: GPS is used for establishing primary horizontal control, densification, and surveying accessible surface areas.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The main limitation of GPS in mine surveying is:
options: It cannot be used underground or in areas without open sky view
questions.solution: GPS requires clear sky visibility; it cannot work in deep pits, underground mines, or dense forest cover.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: Differential GPS (DGPS) improves accuracy by:
options: Using two GPS receivers — one as base and one as rover
questions.solution: DGPS uses a base station at a known position to compute corrections applied to the rover, improving accuracy.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: RTK (Real-Time Kinematic) GPS provides:
questions.solution: RTK GPS uses carrier-phase measurements with a base station to provide centimetre-level accuracy in real time.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The 'baseline' in GPS surveying refers to:
options: The vector between two simultaneously observed GPS points
questions.solution: A GPS baseline is the three-dimensional vector between two points observed simultaneously.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: In a GPS control survey, 'static' observation means:
options: Receivers are left on fixed points for extended periods (hours) for high accuracy
questions.solution: Static GPS involves long-duration observations (1-24 hours) at fixed points for the highest accuracy.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: A 'strong triangle figure' in triangulation is one in which:
options: Angles are well-distributed between 30° and 120° with good geometry
questions.solution: Strong triangle figures have well-conditioned angles (30°-120°) that minimize error propagation.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: In triangulation, the 'forward direction' is determined by:
options: Observing angles from a known station to an unknown station
questions.solution: Forward direction involves measuring angles from a known station to determine the direction to the next unknown station.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: A 'braced quadrilateral' in triangulation is:
options: A triangle with an extra diagonal
A four-sided figure with both diagonals measured, providing strong geometry
questions.solution: A braced quadrilateral has both diagonals observed, providing redundancy and strong geometric strength.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The 'base line measurement' in old triangulation surveys was done using:
options: Precision丈量 (taping) with steel bands or invar wires
questions.solution: Historically, base lines were measured with invar tapes/wires under precise tension and temperature conditions.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The modern method for base line measurement in control surveys is:
questions.solution: EDM is now the standard for precise base line measurement in control surveys.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: In a triangulation network, 'side equation' check ensures:
options: The length computed through different paths of triangles agrees
questions.solution: Side equations verify that distances computed through different chains of triangles yield consistent results.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: In mine control surveys, the 'primary control' network:
options: Covers the entire mine in detail
Provides the main reference framework with the highest accuracy
questions.solution: Primary control is the highest-accuracy network from which secondary and tertiary surveys are derived.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: GPS surveying in open-pit mines is used for:
options: Rapid topographic surveys, volume calculations, and equipment tracking
questions.solution: GPS enables rapid topographic surveys, volume calculations, and real-time equipment tracking in open-pit mines.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The 'WGS 84' coordinate system is:
options: The World Geodetic System used as the reference frame for GPS
questions.solution: WGS 84 (World Geodetic System 1984) is the global reference coordinate system used by GPS.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: Converting GPS coordinates (lat/lon) to a local mine grid requires:
options: A map projection and datum transformation
questions.solution: GPS geodetic coordinates must be transformed using a map projection (e.g., UTM) and datum conversion to local grid.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: In triangulation, 'angular misclosure' is distributed using:
options: Equal distribution or condensation adjustment (least squares)
questions.solution: Angular misclosure is distributed equally (simple) or by least squares adjustment (rigorous) for high-accuracy surveys.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The altitude of a celestial body is its angular distance
options: Above or below the observer's horizon
questions.solution: Angular distance above or below the horizon.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The azimuth of a celestial body is measured from
options: The north or south point along the horizon
questions.solution: Measured from north or south point along the horizon.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The hour angle of a celestial body is
options: The angle measured westward from the observer's meridian
questions.solution: Angle measured westward from the observer's meridian.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The declination of a star is analogous to
questions.solution: Analogous to latitude on Earth.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The zenith distance of a star is
questions.solution: Zenith distance = 90 - altitude.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The astronomical triangle is formed by
questions.solution: Formed by zenith, celestial pole, and star.

questions.stem: Sidereal time is based on the
questions.solution: Based on stars' apparent motion.

questions.stem: A sidereal day is shorter than a solar day by approximately

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: Local Mean Time (LMT) is based on
questions.solution: Based on the observer's longitude.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: Local Sidereal Time (LST) is the
options: Hour angle of the vernal equinox
questions.solution: Hour angle of the vernal equinox.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The equal altitude method for finding true bearing involves
options: Observing a star at equal altitudes east and west of the meridian
questions.solution: Observing star at equal altitudes east and west.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The gyro theodolite determines
questions.solution: Determines true north direction.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The gyro north is determined by
questions.solution: By free gyroscope precession.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: A free gyroscope maintains its axis in
questions.solution: Maintains axis in the same plane in space.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The precession of a gyroscope is the
options: Slow rotation of the spin axis about a vertical axis
questions.solution: Slow rotation of spin axis about vertical axis.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The meridian altitude of a star is its altitude when it is
questions.solution: When on the observer's meridian.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The zenith is the point directly
options: Above the observer on the celestial sphere
questions.solution: Directly above the observer on celestial sphere.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The celestial equator is the projection of
options: Earth's equator onto the celestial sphere
questions.solution: Projection of Earth's equator onto celestial sphere.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The ecliptic is the apparent path of the
questions.solution: Apparent path of the Sun on celestial sphere.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) is based on
questions.solution: Based on the prime meridian.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: Universal Time (UT) is essentially the same as
questions.solution: Essentially the same as GMT.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The conversion from LMT to GMT requires knowledge of
questions.solution: The observer's longitude.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The Polaris is useful for azimuth determination because
options: It is very close to the north celestial pole
questions.solution: Very close to the north celestial pole.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The co-latitude of a place is
questions.solution: Co-latitude = 90 - latitude.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: In the astronomical triangle, the three vertices are
questions.solution: Zenith, north celestial pole, and star.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The time equation is the difference between
options: Apparent solar time and mean solar time
questions.solution: Between apparent solar time and mean solar time.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The gyro theodolite operates on the principle of
options: Conservation of angular momentum of a spinning rotor
questions.solution: Conservation of angular momentum of spinning rotor.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The meridian passage of a star occurs when it
questions.solution: Crosses the observer's meridian.

questions.subject: Mine Surveying
questions.stem: The prime vertical is the great circle passing through the zenith and
questions.solution: Through zenith and east-west points.
